paragraphs: Anyone who hurries to marry immediately after becoming a bar mitzvah is praiseworthy, for the Gemara (Kiddushin 29b) says: Rav Chisda said, "The reason I am superior to my colleagues is that I married at sixteen; had I married at fourteen, I would have said to the Evil Inclination, an arrow in your eye." Therefore every person should be diligent in this matter and will be rewarded. However, before the age of fourteen, which has not yet reached the years of majority, it is not fitting to marry; and if one has some compelling reason to marry earlier, let him consult our teacher Rabbi Yom Tov Alnaqua, of blessed memory, in "Simchat Yom Tov," as to how to proceed regarding the ketubah.

clarification.explanation: One who hurries to marry immediately after becoming bar mitzvah is praiseworthy. The Gemara (Kiddushin 29b) brings the words of Rav Chisda, who said that he is superior to his colleagues because he married at the age of sixteen, whereas had he married at fourteen he could have said to the Evil Inclination, "an arrow in your eye," and would not have feared it at all. Therefore it is fitting for every person to be diligent in this matter. However, before the age of fourteen, when one has not yet reached the years of majority, it is not proper to marry. And if there is a compelling reason to marry earlier, one should consult the book Simchat Yom Tov by our teacher Rabbi Yom Tov Alnaqua as to how to proceed regarding the ketubah.
takeaways: It is fitting to hurry and marry close to the age of bar mitzvah, and diligence in this is praiseworthy
One should not marry before the age of fourteen, which is the age of majority
Marrying early helps a person stand against the Evil Inclination

paragraphs: Just as one recites the blessing over enjoyment (birkat ha-nehenin) over anything from which one is about to benefit before benefiting from it, so too one recites a blessing over the benefit of the wife before the betrothal (erusin); therefore our Sages, of blessed memory, instituted the blessing of erusin. By strict law, if a man betroths a woman himself, he recites the blessing; and if through an agent, the agent recites it in his place. However, in many places the custom is that the groom does not recite the blessing, but rather the one who arranges the kiddushin recites it, so that one who does not know how to recite the blessing should not be embarrassed. Thus the blessing recited by the other person is meant to discharge the groom's obligation, since the obligation of the blessing rests upon him. Therefore the one reciting the blessing must be careful to intend to discharge the groom's obligation, and the groom too must pay close attention to the blessing and intend to fulfill his obligation through it. It is also good to caution the bride to direct her attention and hear the blessing, and that the one reciting it intend for her as well — see Beit Shmuel, siman 34, se'if katan 2, and Noda BiYehudah, second edition, Even HaEzer siman 1, and other later authorities who wrote on this. According to the Rambam, if the one reciting the blessing did not intend to discharge the obligation and the groom did not intend to fulfill it, the blessing is in vain. And although Rav Be'er Sheva, of blessed memory, page 111, wrote a different reason — that this is a blessing of praise and thanksgiving over the holiness of Israel, see there, and see Knesset HaGedolah — and according to this reasoning, if the groom did not intend, there is no problem; nevertheless one must be concerned for the view of the halachic authorities who wrote the first reason, and all the more so since according to the great authority, the Rambam, of blessed memory, intent is required.

clarification.explanation: Just as one recites birkat ha-nehenin over anything one is about to enjoy before enjoying it, so too our Sages instituted a blessing over the benefit of the wife before the betrothal — the blessing of erusin. By strict law, if the one betrothing does so himself, he recites the blessing; if through an agent, the agent recites it in his place. But in many places the custom is that the groom does not recite the blessing, but rather the one arranging the kiddushin recites it, so that one who does not know how to recite it should not be embarrassed. Therefore the one reciting the blessing must intend to discharge the groom's obligation, and the groom must pay close attention to the blessing and intend to fulfill it through it. It is also good for the bride to intend and listen to the blessing, with the one reciting it intending for her as well. According to the Rambam, if the one reciting the blessing did not intend to discharge the obligation and the groom did not intend to fulfill it, the blessing is found to be in vain, and therefore one must be careful about this intent.
takeaways: The blessing of erusin was instituted over the benefit of the wife, similar to birkat ha-nehenin
The custom is that the one arranging the kiddushin recites the blessing instead of the groom, so that one who does not know how should not be embarrassed
The one reciting the blessing must intend to discharge the groom's obligation, and the groom must intend to fulfill it

paragraphs: The custom is to arrange the blessing of erusin over wine, since it is a blessing of joy. One first recites over the wine "Borei peri hagafen," and afterward recites the blessing of erusin. If no wine is available, one recites the blessing of erusin alone, without wine. The blessing of erusin concludes with "Who sanctifies His people Israel through chuppah by means of kiddushin," and this is the true wording, more correct than the other version which says "through chuppah and kiddushin," and it is the version agreed upon in the Shulchan Aruch, whose rulings we have accepted. However, if there is a place with a known custom to say "through chuppah and kiddushin," one should not nullify their custom, for they have a basis to rely upon.

clarification.explanation: The custom is to arrange the blessing of erusin over wine, because it is a blessing of joy. One first recites over the wine "Borei peri hagafen" and then recites the blessing of erusin. If there is no wine, one recites only the blessing of erusin, without wine. The blessing concludes "Who sanctifies His people Israel through chuppah by means of kiddushin," and this is the truer and more precise wording, and it is the version agreed upon in the Shulchan Aruch, whose rulings we have accepted. However, a place that has a known custom to say "through chuppah and kiddushin" should not have its custom nullified, since they have a basis to rely upon.
takeaways: The blessing of erusin is arranged over wine because it is a blessing of joy
In the absence of wine, one recites only the blessing of erusin
The precise concluding wording is "through chuppah by means of kiddushin," but a place that follows a different custom should not have it nullified

paragraphs: As for what is said in this blessing, "and has permitted to us those who are married to us" — although Maran, of blessed memory, did not write it so in the Shulchan Aruch, nevertheless this wording is more precise and clear, as the Gaon Bayit Chadash wrote: that if one does not say "those who are married to us" but says simply "those who are married," it implies that what is permitted are those married to others through chuppah and kiddushin. Therefore it is preferable to say "those who are married to us," and so we are accustomed to do here in our city — see the later authorities. And what is written, "and has forbidden to us the betrothed," the intent is to say that even women who have become betrothed are forbidden to their betrothed by rabbinic law until they enter the chuppah.

clarification.explanation: In the blessing of erusin one says "and has permitted to us those who are married to us." Although Maran did not write it so in the Shulchan Aruch, this wording is more precise and clear, as the Bach wrote: that if one does not say "those who are married to us" but says simply "those who are married," it implies that what was permitted is those married to others through chuppah and kiddushin. Therefore it is preferable to say "those who are married to us," and so we are accustomed to do in our city. And what is said, "and has forbidden to us the betrothed," means that even women who have already become betrothed are forbidden to their betrothed by rabbinic law until they enter the chuppah.
takeaways: It is preferable to say in the blessing "those who are married to us" — a precise wording that prevents a mistaken meaning
The meaning of "and has forbidden to us the betrothed" is that a betrothed woman is forbidden to her betrothed until the chuppah
The prohibition on a betrothed woman before the chuppah is by rabbinic law

paragraphs: After the blessing and the tasting of the cup, the groom shall show the kiddushin money to the witnesses so that they know it is worth at least a perutah, and the witnesses must set their eyes to see the giving of the kiddushin money into the bride's hand, since it is through their witnessing this that she becomes betrothed. And one must caution the bride to look at the face of the groom who is betrothing her, and to pay attention at the time the money is given into her hand, and to accept it for the sake of kiddushin. For there are brides who are very shy, and at the time of the kiddushin they are almost about to faint, and the bride does not pay attention to what the groom says to her at the time of the kiddushin, nor to the handing over of the money into her hand; therefore one must caution them about this.

clarification.explanation: After the blessing and the tasting of the cup, the groom shows the kiddushin money to the witnesses so that they know it is worth at least a perutah, and the witnesses must set their eyes to see the money being given into the bride's hand, since it is through their witnessing this that she becomes betrothed. One must caution the bride to look at the face of the groom betrothing her and to pay attention when he gives the money into her hand, and to accept it for the sake of kiddushin. For there are brides who are very shy, and at the time of the kiddushin they nearly faint and do not pay attention to what the groom says to them or to the handing over of the money, and therefore one must caution them about this.
takeaways: The groom shows the kiddushin money to the witnesses so they know it is worth at least a perutah
The witnesses must see the money given into the bride's hand, for this is what effects the kiddushin
One must caution the bride to pay attention and accept the money for the sake of kiddushin

paragraphs: He shall first say, "Behold, you are betrothed to me with this, according to the law of Moses and Israel," and afterward give her the kiddushin money. But he should not give her the kiddushin money first and afterward say the aforementioned words, because that would be regarded as betrothing by way of a loan. And what is written, "according to the law of Moses and Israel," the intent is: because whoever betroths does so with the understanding of the Sages, meaning, in accordance with what our Sages instituted in Israel does he betroth her — that the kiddushin be valid according to the words of the Sages, and be nullified according to the words of the Sages by means of the divorce documents that the Sages arranged.

clarification.explanation: First the groom shall say, "Behold, you are betrothed to me with this, according to the law of Moses and Israel," and only afterward give her the kiddushin money. But he should not give the money first and only afterward say the words, because that is then considered betrothing by means of a loan. And what is said, "according to the law of Moses and Israel," means that whoever betroths does so with the understanding of the Sages — that is, in accordance with what the Sages instituted in Israel — so that the kiddushin will be valid according to their words, and will be nullified according to their words, by means of the divorce document that the Sages arranged.
takeaways: The wording of the kiddushin should be said first, and only afterward should the money be given
Giving the money before the declaration is considered betrothing by means of a loan
"According to the law of Moses and Israel" teaches that the one betrothing does so with the understanding of the Sages

paragraphs: He shall give the kiddushin money from his right hand to her right hand. And here in our city, Baghdad, may it be protected, the custom when betrothing with silver or gold is to wrap the bride's hand in a silk kerchief, and she receives the kiddushin money in her hand while it is wrapped. The reason for this custom is as a good omen, that she should receive the money of her kiddushin with honor, following the same reasoning given for the cloth on the table on Shabbat, when the two loaves of bread are arranged upon it, so that it should not appear as though it were a poor woman receiving charity in her hand. See Kerem Shlomo Ashkenazi, Even HaEzer section, in the Responsa at the end of the book, siman 86, where he was particular about this as an initial requirement because of the concern of an interposition (chatzitzah), and in the holy work Miqabtziel I wrote on this matter.

clarification.explanation: The groom gives the kiddushin money from his right hand to the bride's right hand. And here in our city Baghdad, the custom, when betrothing with silver or gold, is to wrap the bride's hand in a silk kerchief, and she receives the money in her wrapped hand. The reason for the custom is as a good omen, so that she should receive the money of her kiddushin with honor, similar to the reason given for the cloth placed on the table on Shabbat on which the two loaves of bread are set, so that it should not appear as though she were a poor woman receiving charity in her hand. Some were particular about this as an initial requirement, out of concern for an interposition.
takeaways: The kiddushin money is given from the groom's right hand to the bride's right hand
In Baghdad the custom is to wrap the bride's hand in a silk kerchief, as a sign of honor
Some were particular about this as an initial requirement, out of concern for an interposition

paragraphs: Some have the custom of betrothing with three coins, of gold, silver, and copper, but it appears that it is the most preferable way of fulfilling the mitzvah to betroth with a silver ring. And there is a proper allusion in the ring, as I wrote in the holy work Miqabtziel, based on what our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, wrote in Sha'ar Ta'amei HaMitzvot, parashat Ki Tetze: that through the kiddushin by which a man betroths his wife, a single spirit is drawn to her from the power of the husband's spirit, in the aspect of an encompassing light (or makif) from his own spirit; afterward, when he comes to her in complete union, he gives her a spirit in the secret of an inner light within her, from the power of his own spirit. Therefore the kiddushin must precede, since the inner spirit does not enter her until the encompassing light enters — see there. Accordingly, in a ring, which encompasses the finger, there is a proper allusion to the encompassing light given to her through the kiddushin, and therefore the ring is the most preferable way of fulfilling the mitzvah. Our custom is to engrave on the ring the shape of the letter heh, and this is a beautiful custom. And here in our city, in these days, this custom of betrothing with a ring has spread more widely, though there are still many who betroth with silver or gold given into the hand; and when betrothing with a ring, the custom is not to wrap the hand in a kerchief, and from this aspect too there is found to be a preference for the ring.

clarification.explanation: Some have the custom of betrothing with three coins, of gold, silver, and copper; and it appears that the most preferable way of fulfilling the mitzvah is to betroth with a silver ring. And there is a proper allusion in the ring (as the Ben Ish Chai wrote in Miqabtziel, based on the Ari in Sha'ar Ta'amei HaMitzvot): through the kiddushin, a "spirit" is drawn to the wife from the power of the husband's spirit, in the aspect of an "encompassing light"; and afterward, through complete union, a "spirit" is given to her in the aspect of an "inner light"; and the kiddushin must precede, since the inner light does not enter her until the encompassing light enters. Accordingly, the ring, which encompasses the finger, alludes beautifully to the encompassing light given to her through the kiddushin — and therefore it is the most preferable way of fulfilling the mitzvah. Our custom is to engrave on the ring the shape of the letter heh — a beautiful custom. In our city the custom of betrothing with a ring has spread, and there are others who still betroth with silver and gold given into the hand; and when betrothing with a ring, the custom is not to wrap the hand in a kerchief — and in this respect too there is an advantage to the ring.
takeaways: It is the most preferable way of fulfilling the mitzvah to betroth with a silver ring — which alludes to the 'encompassing light' drawn to the wife in the kiddushin (per the Ari's teaching)
It is a beautiful custom to engrave the letter heh on the ring; and when betrothing with a ring, the hand is not wrapped in a kerchief

paragraphs: When betrothing with a ring, according to what appears from the words of the Tikkunim, based on the esoteric tradition, it is fitting to place the ring on the third finger, called the amah (the middle finger). But here in our city the custom is to place the ring on the finger next to the thumb, called simply "the finger" (the index finger), and elsewhere I gave a reason for this too, based on the esoteric tradition. And in the book Kemach Solet a reason for this is explained: that in the psalm "The heavens declare the glory of God" (Psalms 19:2), where the chuppah of the groom is mentioned, as it is written, "and he is as a groom coming forth from his chuppah," there are five verses whose second word is the Name of Havayah, and they are the verses "The Torah of the Lord is perfect...," "The testimony of the Lord is sure...," "The precepts of the Lord are right...," "The commandment of the Lord is pure...," "The fear of the Lord is clean...." And when one begins counting these words from the thumb, the blessed Name falls upon the finger next to the thumb. And it is known that in the mitzvah of kiddushin there is a unification of the Name: the ring itself corresponds to the yod, the groom's hand which holds it with its five fingers corresponds to the first heh, the bride's finger corresponds to the vav, and her hand which is extended to receive the kiddushin corresponds to the final heh — as it is written (Proverbs 18:22), "He who finds a wife finds good, and obtains favor from the Lord." Therefore, since a unification of the Name Havayah is thereby effected, he shall place the ring on the finger next to the thumb, which corresponds to the Name Havayah — see there. And I have heard that also in the holy city of Jerusalem, may it be rebuilt and reestablished, the custom is to place the ring on the finger next to the thumb.

clarification.explanation: According to the esoteric tradition it is fitting to place the ring on the third finger, called the amah, but our custom is to place the ring on the finger next to the thumb (the index finger). The book Kemach Solet gives a reason for this based on the psalm "The heavens declare the glory of God," in which the chuppah of the groom is mentioned, and which contains five verses whose second word is the Name Havayah. When one begins counting these words from the thumb, it turns out that the Name Havayah falls on the finger next to the thumb. And in the act of kiddushin a unification of the Name is effected: the ring corresponds to the yod, the groom's hand to the first heh, the bride's finger to the vav, and the bride's outstretched hand to the final heh. Therefore the ring is placed on the finger next to the thumb, which corresponds to the Name Havayah. And I have heard that in Jerusalem too the custom is to place the ring on the finger next to the thumb.
takeaways: According to the esoteric tradition it is fitting to place the ring on the middle finger, but the custom is to place it on the finger next to the thumb
In the act of kiddushin, a unification of the Name Havayah between the groom and bride is alluded to
In Jerusalem too the custom is to place the ring on the finger next to the thumb

paragraphs: If the blessing of erusin was not recited at the time of the kiddushin, it should not be recited at the nissuin (marriage). And although there are those who hold that it should be recited, we maintain that in a case of doubt regarding blessings, the lenient view is followed. Nevertheless, it is good to teach the groom, for whom the blessing was not recited at the time of erusin, that he himself should recite it quietly at the time of the chuppah, without mentioning God's Name and Sovereignty. And one who fears Heaven should strive with all his might not to become betrothed without the blessing, and should understand that this blessing occurs only once in his entire life, and how much a person must be careful not to lose it through his own doing, unlike the practice of certain ignorant people who follow the superstitions of women in this matter. And one who is careful in this will have a blessing of good come upon him.

clarification.explanation: If the blessing of erusin was not recited at the time of the kiddushin, it should not be recited at the time of the nissuin either, for although there are those who hold it should be recited, we maintain the rule that in a case of doubt regarding blessings, the lenient view is followed. Nevertheless, it is good to teach the groom for whom the blessing was not recited at the time of erusin that he himself should recite it quietly at the time of the chuppah, without mentioning God's Name and Sovereignty. And one who fears Heaven should strive with all his strength not to become betrothed without the blessing, and should understand that this blessing occurs only once in his lifetime, and one must be very careful not to lose it deliberately, as is the practice of certain ignorant people who follow the superstitions of women in this matter.
takeaways: If the blessing of erusin was not recited at the kiddushin, it is not recited at the nissuin, following the rule of doubt regarding blessings
The groom may recite it quietly at the time of the chuppah without mentioning God's Name and Sovereignty
One must be very careful not to forgo this blessing on account of superstitions

paragraphs: After the kiddushin, the groom breaks a cup in remembrance of Jerusalem, as it is written (Psalms 137:5), "If I forget you, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget its skill... if I do not set Jerusalem above my chief joy." And it is good, when breaking the cup, to say quietly, "I will set Jerusalem above my chief joy." And here in our city the custom is that the groom breaks a small new cup, of the kind used for drinking coffee, made of clean glazed earthenware, which is good, and is called "parpuri" (with a tin glaze). And the custom is not to break a glass cup, called "balur" (fine glass), and it may be either because it costs ten times as much or more than this parpuri cup, or perhaps because of concern for mishap from the small shards of glass that scatter on the ground, since the cup is broken at the height of the wall and small shards are made and fall to the ground. And the Rema, of blessed memory, in Darkhei Moshe, siman 560, wrote that the groom breaks the cup over which the blessing of erusin was recited, and therefore the custom is to recite the blessing of erusin over an earthenware cup. It thus emerges that the Rav took an earthenware cup and did not take a glass one, and in his words too both reasons mentioned may be attached. And the Gaon Mishbetzot Zahav, in siman 560, brought from Even HaShoham that glass is required, and gave a reason for this in the name of our teacher Rabbi Moshe Tirani, of blessed memory: that they thereby allude, with glass, to the fact that it has a remedy after being broken, in that one may go back and repair it — which is not so with earthenware. See Mo'ed LeChol Chai, siman yud, letter 96. However this may be, the custom of our city with an earthenware vessel is explicit in the words of the aforementioned Rema, and it should not be changed. And the custom is as follows: if the betrothal takes place several days before the chuppah and the blessing of erusin is recited over the cup, then after the one reciting the blessing drinks, he pours a little wine remaining in that cup into this small cup, and gives a taste from this small cup to the bride, and then the groom takes the small cup and breaks it against the wall. And if the kiddushin is performed at the time of the chuppah, they do the same. And afterward they bring a second cup of wine and recite over it the seven blessings of the chuppah, and no other cup is broken. And if the groom became betrothed several days before the chuppah without a cup, then when they perform the chuppah and recite the seven blessings and the one reciting the blessing drinks, they pour from the remainder of the cup into the small earthenware cup, and the bride tastes it, and afterward the groom takes the small cup and breaks it against the wall.

clarification.explanation:
After the kiddushin the groom breaks a cup in remembrance of the destruction of Jerusalem, based on the verse "If I forget you, O Jerusalem... if I do not set Jerusalem above my chief joy." And it is good that at the time of breaking the cup he say quietly, "I will set Jerusalem above my chief joy." In our city the custom is to break a small glazed earthenware cup (of the kind used for drinking coffee), and not a glass cup, perhaps because the glass cup is far more expensive, or because of concern for mishap from the small glass shards that scatter on the floor when the groom breaks the cup at the height of the wall. The Rema wrote that the groom breaks the cup over which the blessing of erusin was recited, and therefore the custom is to recite the blessing of erusin over an earthenware cup. Some wrote that glass specifically is required, to allude to the fact that just as glass has a remedy after being broken, so too repair is possible — which is not so with earthenware. But the custom of our city with an earthenware vessel is explicit in the words of the Rema and should not be changed.
And this is the order of the procedure: if the kiddushin is performed several days before the chuppah and the blessing of erusin is recited over the cup — after the one reciting the blessing drinks, he pours a little of the remaining wine from the cup into the small cup, gives a taste of it to the bride, and then the groom takes the small cup and breaks it against the wall. The same is done if the kiddushin takes place at the time of the chuppah. Afterward a second cup of wine is brought and the seven blessings are recited over it — and no other cup is broken (only one cup is broken). And if he became betrothed several days before the chuppah without a cup — when they perform the chuppah and recite the seven blessings and the one reciting the blessing drinks, they pour from the remainder of the cup into the small earthenware cup, the bride tastes it, and afterward the groom takes the small cup and breaks it against the wall.
takeaways: The groom breaks a cup after the kiddushin in remembrance of the destruction of Jerusalem
It is good to say quietly at the time of breaking, "I will set Jerusalem above my chief joy"
In our city the custom is to break a small earthenware cup, not glass, following the view of the Rema

Order of the procedure: after the one reciting the blessing drinks, they pour from the remainder into the small cup, give the bride a taste, and the groom breaks it against the wall; for the seven blessings a second cup is brought — and only one cup is broken.

paragraphs: Our Sages, of blessed memory, forbade a man to come upon his betrothed before her entry into the chuppah. And the Rema, of blessed memory, wrote in the gloss on the Shulchan Aruch that the simple custom now is to call "chuppah" the place where a sheet or tallit is spread over poles, and the groom and bride are brought beneath it in public, and he betroths her there and they recite there the blessing of erusin and the blessing of nissuin; and afterward they are led to their home and the groom and bride eat together in a modest place — and this is the chuppah as practiced now, so far his words. And in the holy city of Jerusalem, may it be rebuilt and reestablished, the custom is that the groom wears a fringed tallit properly, in the blessing of erusin, and afterward, before the blessings of nissuin, they cast the tallit also over the head of the bride, so that it is spread over the groom and his bride together, and this is their chuppah. And here in our city, Baghdad, may it be protected, the custom is to spread a curtain in front of the bride at the time of the seven blessings of nissuin, which are recited after the blessing of erusin, and this curtain is called in Arabic "kidir" (bridal canopy), spread as a partition in front of the bride, between her and the groom and the one reciting the blessing, and the custom is not to wear a tallit. And perhaps the reason we are not accustomed to a tallit is that here in our city the chuppah and seven blessings are performed after the evening prayer, at sunset, or after sunset, or even until full darkness, and it is not fitting to wear a tallit at that time. And this curtain is the sign of the chuppah among us, for all the things done at the time of the chuppah are only a sign that they are doing something that shows that he is designating her to bring her into his home and setting her apart to be his full wife; and among us, the spreading of the curtain called in Arabic "kidir" is the sign for this matter. And some years ago we discontinued this curtain and made in its place four posts over which a cloth was spread like a canopy spread over four poles, and the groom and bride were stood together beneath it; and afterward this custom fell into disuse, and we returned to instructing them to make a curtain as in the earlier custom.

clarification.explanation: Our Sages forbade a man to come upon his betrothed before she enters the chuppah. The Rema wrote that the simple custom now is to call "chuppah" the place where a sheet or tallit is spread over poles, and the groom and bride are brought beneath it in public, and he betroths her and they recite there the blessing of erusin and the blessing of nissuin, and afterward they are led to their home and eat together in a modest place. In Jerusalem the custom is that the groom wears a fringed tallit at the blessing of erusin, and afterward, before the blessings of nissuin, they cast the tallit also over the bride's head, so that it is spread over both of them together — and this is their chuppah. And here in our city, Baghdad, the custom is to spread a curtain in front of the bride at the time of the seven blessings of nissuin, and this curtain (called in Arabic "kidir") is the sign of the chuppah among us. All the things done at the time of the chuppah are only a sign that the groom is designating the bride to bring her into his home and setting her apart to be his full wife.
takeaways: It is forbidden to come upon the betrothed before her entry into the chuppah
There are various customs for the form of the chuppah: a sheet on poles, a tallit, or a curtain
The acts of the chuppah are a sign of the groom designating the bride to be his full wife

paragraphs: The custom is that the groom fasts on the day he enters the chuppah, because one who marries has his sins forgiven, and it is fitting that along with this there also be the merit of fasting; and further, so that through the fast he will have a broken heart, more conducive to accepting repentance. And here in our city many are accustomed to this, but specifically the groom — the brides are not accustomed to this, and it has never happened that any bride fasted before the chuppah at all.

clarification.explanation: The custom is that the groom fasts on the day he enters the chuppah, because one who marries has his sins forgiven, and it is fitting that along with the forgiveness there also be the merit of a fast, and further, so that through the fast he will have a broken heart conducive to accepting repentance. In our city many are accustomed to this, but specifically the groom and not the bride, and it has never happened that a bride fasted before the chuppah at all.
takeaways: The groom fasts on the day he enters the chuppah, since his sins are forgiven
The fast adds merit and brings about a broken heart and repentance
Brides are not accustomed to fasting before the chuppah

paragraphs: The blessing of erusin, at the outset, requires ten men; but after the fact, if ten did not happen to be present, it is permitted to recite the blessing without ten. But the seven blessings of the chuppah require ten, and this is not permitted even after the fact. And if one is in a country where there are not ten men in the entire country, and he cannot go to another city for compelling reasons, one may rely on the lenient authorities to perform the chuppah there and recite specifically the blessing "Who has created." However, if afterward it happens that the man and his wife come to another city, they should both go and stand near a chuppah that is in that city, and hear the seven blessings, and intend to discharge their own obligation as well. So I have concluded in the holy work Miqabtziel; and see the Gaon Chida, of blessed memory, in Kise Rachamim and in Kikar LeAden.

clarification.explanation: The blessing of erusin at the outset requires ten men, but after the fact, if ten did not happen to be present, one may recite the blessing even without them. But the seven blessings of the chuppah require ten, and this is not possible even after the fact. And if one is in a country where there are no ten men at all, and cannot go to another city for compelling reasons, one may rely on the lenient authorities to perform the chuppah there and recite specifically the blessing "Who has created." And if afterward the man and his wife happen to come to another city, they should both go and stand near a chuppah in that city, and hear the seven blessings, and intend to discharge their own obligation through them.
takeaways: The blessing of erusin at the outset requires ten, but after the fact it may be recited without them
The seven blessings of the chuppah require ten even after the fact
Where there are no ten at all, one recites only "Who has created," and completes it afterward if possible

paragraphs: After the seven blessings of the chuppah, when a feast is held, the seven blessings are recited over a cup after the Grace After Meals. And at every feast held after the first feast, one must also be careful to recite the seven blessings over a cup after the Grace After Meals; but at each feast "new faces" are required — that is, two people present at that feast who did not eat with them before this — and it is good to seek out important people, for whose sake many will attend. But on Shabbat and Yom Tov, new faces are not required, and one must be careful to recite the seven blessings after the Grace After Meals only where there are ten; but if there are not ten, in which case one does not recite blessings with God's Name, one does not recite the full blessing but only the blessing "Who has created" alone. Nevertheless, even if there is no zimun with God's Name, one must say in the zimun, "in Whose abode is joy."

clarification.explanation: After the seven blessings of the chuppah, when a feast is held, the seven blessings are recited over a cup after the Grace After Meals. And likewise at every feast held after the first feast, one must be careful to recite the seven blessings over a cup after the Grace After Meals, but each feast requires "new faces" — that is, two people present at the feast who did not eat with them before, and it is good to seek out important people for whose sake many rejoice. But on Shabbat and Yom Tov new faces are not required. And the seven blessings after the Grace After Meals are recited only when there are ten; if there are not ten, one recites only "Who has created" alone. And even if there is no zimun with God's Name, one must still say in the zimun "in Whose abode is joy."
takeaways: At every wedding feast the seven blessings are recited over a cup after the Grace After Meals
"New faces" are required at every feast, except on Shabbat and Yom Tov
Without ten, one recites only "Who has created," and says "in Whose abode is joy" in the zimun

paragraphs: The groom, throughout the seven days of the wedding feast, shall not perform work, even regarding something that would otherwise be lost; nor shall he engage in business in the market, nor go out alone into the market, because the groom is comparable to a king: just as a king does not perform work and does not go out alone, so too the groom; rather, he eats and drinks and rejoices with his bride, whether he is a young unmarried man or a widower who married a virgin — and the wife cannot waive her right to her joy. But the groom's business partner may perform work or engage in commerce and give the groom his share, for this differs from the law of a mourner, may the Merciful One save us. And a widower who marries a widow or divorcée must rejoice with her for three days, but a young unmarried man who marries a widow or divorcée must rejoice for seven days; and one who remarries his divorced wife must rejoice for three days, like a widow.

clarification.explanation: The groom, throughout the seven days of the wedding feast, shall not perform work, even regarding something that might otherwise be lost, nor engage in business in the market, nor go out alone into the market, because the groom is comparable to a king: just as a king does not perform work and does not go out alone, so too the groom; rather he eats and drinks and rejoices with his bride. This applies whether he is a young unmarried man or a widower who married a virgin, and the wife cannot waive her right to her joy. But the groom's partner may perform work or engage in commerce and give the groom his share. A widower who marries a widow or divorcée must rejoice with her for three days, a young unmarried man who marries her for seven days, and one who remarries his divorced wife rejoices for three days, like with a widow.
takeaways: The groom is comparable to a king: he does not perform work and does not go out alone during the seven days of the wedding feast
The wife cannot waive her right to her days of joy
The length of the days of joy varies according to the status of the groom and bride, between three and seven days

paragraphs: A groom for whom the Seventeenth of Tammuz, the Fast of Gedaliah, the Tenth of Tevet, or the Fast of Esther occurs within the seven days of his chuppah — some say he should fast and complete the fast, and some say he should not fast. And here in our city the custom is that he does not fast. And if a yahrzeit occurs for him, all agree he should not fast, since it is his own festive day.

clarification.explanation: A groom for whom one of the four minor fasts — the Seventeenth of Tammuz, the Fast of Gedaliah, the Tenth of Tevet, or the Fast of Esther — occurs within the seven days of his chuppah: some say he should fast and complete the fast, and some say he should not fast. In our city the custom is that he does not fast. And if the yahrzeit of one of his parents occurs during the days of the chuppah, by all opinions he does not fast, because it is his own festive day.
takeaways: In our city the custom is that the groom does not fast on the minor fasts during the seven days of his chuppah
There are those who disagree and hold that he should fast and complete it
On a parent's yahrzeit he does not fast, since these are his days of joy

paragraphs: It is a great mitzvah to gladden the groom and bride, and to say humorous things to them so that they rejoice, and the reward of one who gladdens them is very great; only one must be careful not to gladden them through frivolity or through any prohibition, even a light one, even by rabbinic law. And regarding all that has been written, men and women should not dance together, and even women dancing alone before the men is forbidden, because it arouses the Evil Inclination in the men who watch. And several of the later authorities have cried out against such things, that there is no permission for them on account of the joy of the groom and bride. It is a mitzvah to gladden them with musical instruments, and even if the marriage takes place within twelve months of the passing of the father or mother, the joy of musical instruments should not be withheld from them, for it has already been said (Ketubot 17a) that they move the dead out of the way before the bride. And see Maharil, of blessed memory, who ruled that the chuppah should be performed in a different place in order to have musical instruments that could not be brought to their own place — see there. And here in our city, in the time of the crown of our heads, the Gaon our teacher, my grandfather Rabbi Moshe Chaim, of blessed memory, the community wanted to abolish musical instruments at the joy of the groom and bride, and my teacher and grandfather, of blessed memory, did not wish to agree to this. And on the Sabbath day it is forbidden to bring gentiles to play musical instruments, and several later authorities have cried out against this. And here in our city there was an ancient custom from earlier times that when the groom left the synagogue in the morning to go to his home, gentiles would go before him playing musical instruments, and also in his home they would play for about half an hour; and praised be the blessed God, some years ago this custom was entirely discontinued and shall be neither remembered nor missed again.

clarification.explanation: It is a great mitzvah to gladden the groom and bride and to say humorous things before them so that they rejoice, and the reward of one who gladdens them is very great. But one must be careful not to gladden them through frivolity or through any prohibition, even a light one by rabbinic law. And likewise, men and women should not dance together, and even women dancing alone before men is forbidden, because it arouses the Evil Inclination in those who watch, and several rabbis cried out that there is no permission for this on account of the joy of the groom and bride. It is a mitzvah to gladden them with musical instruments, and even if the marriage takes place within twelve months of the passing of a father or mother, the joy of musical instruments should not be withheld. But on Shabbat it is forbidden to bring gentiles to play musical instruments, and several later authorities protested against this.
takeaways: It is a great mitzvah with an immense reward to gladden the groom and bride, but without frivolity and without any prohibition
Mixed dancing of men and women is forbidden, and so is even women's dancing before men
It is a mitzvah to gladden them with musical instruments, but it is forbidden to bring gentiles to play on Shabbat

paragraphs: Regarding what was asked of the Radbaz, of blessed memory, whether a groom is permitted within his [first] year to go out on a business trip to another country, since the verse states (Deuteronomy 24:5), "He shall be free at home one year and shall cheer his wife" — I brought in the holy work Rav Pe'alim the views of the halachic authorities on this matter, and I concluded that if he goes on a business trip for the sake of his livelihood, there is no prohibition here on account of this verse.

clarification.explanation: A question was asked whether a groom is permitted, within his first year, to go on a business trip to another country, since the verse says, "He shall be free at home one year and shall cheer his wife." And our teacher concluded that if he goes on a business trip for the sake of his livelihood, there is no prohibition in this on account of this verse.
takeaways: The verse "He shall be free at home one year" teaches the obligation to cheer the wife in the first year
One who goes on a business trip for the sake of livelihood does not violate this prohibition

paragraphs: A man is permitted to marry the daughter of his father's wife who is from another man, and we are not concerned about appearances, that she might appear to be his sister, since word gets around and everyone knows that she is not his sister. Therefore, Leah and her daughter Dinah are permitted to be married to the father and his son — the father may take Dinah and the son may take Leah, or vice versa. And regarding this law, people say a riddle: a certain woman met a certain child and said to him, "Peace be upon you, my brother"; how is your father's peace, he who is the brother of my son? And the solution to the riddle, on this premise, is that Jacob took Dinah the daughter of Leah, and Reuben, Jacob's son, took Leah the mother of Dinah; and behold, Dinah bore Jacob a son named Simeon, and Leah bore Reuben a son named Levi; and Dinah met Levi, whom Leah bore to Reuben, and called him "my brother," for he is her brother through their mother, who is Leah; and she said, "how is your father's peace" — that is, Reuben, who is the brother of my son Simeon, for Simeon is a brother to Reuben through their father Jacob — and the matter is clear.

clarification.explanation: It is permitted for a man to marry the daughter of his father's wife who is from another man, and we are not concerned about appearances, that she might appear to be his sister, because word gets around and everyone knows she is not truly his sister. Therefore, if Reuben married Leah and Leah has a daughter named Dinah from another man, it is permitted for the father and his son both to marry them — one takes Dinah and the other takes Leah. And upon this law is built a well-known popular riddle, in which a woman meets a child and calls him "my brother," saying that his father is the brother of her son, and all this becomes clear when one combines the family relationships created by these marriages.
takeaways: It is permitted to marry the daughter of one's father's wife who is from another man
We are not concerned about appearances, since everyone knows she is not truly a sister
A father and his son may marry a mother and her daughter, one from the other

paragraphs: A man is permitted to marry the daughter of his father's brother and the daughter of his mother's brother, and we do not issue a decree on account of his father's or mother's sister, since one does not come to confuse them. Likewise, his father's brother and his mother's brother are permitted to marry his wife and his daughter, and we do not issue a decree lest people say, "just as his wife is permitted to them, their wives are also permitted to him," since one does not come to err in this, because the generation has been separated — that is, the relationship has become more distant.

clarification.explanation: It is permitted for a man to marry the daughter of his father's brother (his cousin) and the daughter of his mother's brother, and no decree is issued in this regarding his father's sister and his mother's sister, who are forbidden relations, because one does not come to confuse between them. Likewise, his father's brother and his mother's brother are permitted to marry his wife and his daughter, and no decree is issued lest people say that just as his wife is permitted to them, their wives are also permitted to him, since one does not come to err in this, for the relationship has already become more distant in that generation.
takeaways: It is permitted to marry the daughter of one's father's brother or the daughter of one's mother's brother
No decree is issued regarding them on account of the prohibition of a father's or mother's sister
The distant relationship prevents concern for confusion and substitution

paragraphs: Although there are those who say that even one's father's father's sister, whether on the father's or mother's side, and likewise one's father's mother's sister — in all these no decree was issued, and they are permitted, nevertheless there are those who forbid these, for they hold that a decree is issued regarding them on account of the relation one level closer, namely the sister of one's father or mother, which is a Torah-level forbidden relation. This is unlike the daughter of one's father's brother and the daughter of one's mother's brother of the previous section, where there is no closer or more distant relation that is a Torah-level forbidden relation, and therefore no decree was issued regarding her, since the relationship has become very distant. And since this is a matter of forbidden relations, we follow the position of those who forbid, for we maintain the rule to be stringent in a matter of forbidden relations, even in a case where Maran, of blessed memory, whose rulings we have accepted, ruled simply in accordance with those who permit.

clarification.explanation: There are those who say that even one's father's father's sister and likewise one's father's mother's sister are permitted, and no decree was issued regarding them. But there are those who forbid them, holding that a decree is issued regarding them on account of the closer relation beneath them — namely the sister of one's father or mother, who is a Torah-level forbidden relation. This is not so with the daughter of one's father's brother or the daughter of one's mother's brother discussed in the previous section, where there is no Torah-level forbidden relation either closer or more distant, and therefore no decree was issued regarding her, since the relationship is very distant. And since this is a matter of forbidden relations, we follow the position of those who forbid, for we maintain the rule to be stringent in a matter of forbidden relations, even where Maran ruled simply in accordance with those who permit.
takeaways: The sister of one's father's father and the sister of one's father's mother are forbidden in practice (although there are those who permit them)
Those who forbid are concerned about the closer relation beneath them, which is a Torah-level forbidden relation
In a matter of forbidden relations, one is stringent even when Maran ruled simply to permit

paragraphs: The wife of one's wife's son is permitted to him, and likewise one's wife's son is permitted to marry his wife, for no decree was issued regarding them on account of the wife of one's own son, since word gets around about them and their distant relationship is known, and one does not come to confuse them with one's own son's wife. Likewise, two brothers from one father who are not from one mother, one of whom has a sister from his mother — the other is permitted to marry that sister, as occurred in the time of the Gemara: Rabbi Chiya and Aivu were two brothers from one father named Rav Acha, and Rabbi Chiya had a sister named Imma, who was his sister specifically from his mother and not from his father, and Aivu, who was specifically Rabbi Chiya's brother from their father, married her, and Rav, peace be upon him, was born from Aivu. It thus emerges that Rabbi Chiya was both Rav's father's brother and Rav's mother's brother.

clarification.explanation: The wife of one's wife's son is permitted to him, and likewise one's wife's son is permitted to marry his wife, and no decree was issued regarding them on account of one's own son's wife, because word gets around and everyone knows the relationship is distant, and one does not come to confuse her with one's own son's actual wife. Likewise, two brothers from one father who are not from one mother, one of whom has a sister from his mother — the other is permitted to marry that sister. And so it was in the time of the Gemara: Rabbi Chiya and Aivu were two brothers from one father, and Rabbi Chiya had a sister from his mother named Imma, and Aivu married her, and Rav was born from them. It thus emerges that Rabbi Chiya was both Rav's father's brother and Rav's mother's brother.
takeaways: The wife of one's wife's son and one's wife's son are permitted to one another
No decree was issued regarding them on account of one's own son's wife, because the relationship is known to be distant
An example was brought from Rabbi Chiya, Aivu, and Rav in the Gemara

paragraphs: Two stepbrothers who grow up together in the same house — that is, Jacob married Leah and has a son named Naphtali who was born to him from another wife, and Leah also has a son named Reuben who was born to her from another man — behold, Naphtali and Reuben are called stepbrothers, and even though they grow up together in the house like any two unrelated people, each of them is permitted to marry the other's wife, and we are not concerned about appearances, that it would seem as though he were taking his brother's wife, because word gets around about them and their distant relationship is known, and one does not come to confuse this so as to permit an actual brother's wife.

clarification.explanation: Two stepbrothers who grow up together in one house, such as when Jacob married Leah and has a son named Naphtali from another wife, and Leah has a son named Reuben from another man — Naphtali and Reuben are called stepbrothers. And even though they grow up together in the same house, each of them is permitted to marry the other's wife, and we are not concerned about appearances that it would seem like taking one's brother's wife, because word gets around and everyone knows their relationship is distant, and one does not come through this to permit an actual brother's wife.
takeaways: Two stepbrothers who grow up together are each permitted to marry the other's wife
We are not concerned about the appearance of taking a brother's wife
Everyone knows that there is no actual brotherly relationship between them

paragraphs: Although by strict law a man is permitted to marry the wife of his father-in-law, who is not the mother of his wife, since King David, peace be upon him, married Rizpah the daughter of Aiah, who was the wife of his father-in-law (Sanhedrin 18a), and the same law applies that a father-in-law is permitted to marry his son-in-law's wife — nevertheless there are those who forbid both cases, and say that although King David, peace be upon him, married Rizpah, the wife of his father-in-law, after the time of King David, peace be upon him, our Sages issued a decree on this on account of the appearance that it seems like marrying one's mother-in-law; and likewise a father-in-law should not marry his son-in-law's wife, since it seems like marrying his own daughter. And although there is one who wrote that if his wife dies, he is permitted to take the wife of his father-in-law, who is not the mother of his wife, nevertheless there are halachic authorities who cast doubt on this, and therefore one must rule that even if his wife has died, it is forbidden to take his father-in-law's wife.

clarification.explanation: By strict law it is permitted for a man to marry the wife of his father-in-law who is not the mother of his wife, since King David married Rizpah the daughter of Aiah who was the wife of his father-in-law, and likewise a father-in-law is permitted to marry his son-in-law's wife. But there are those who forbid both cases, saying that although David married her, after his time the Sages issued a decree on this on account of appearances, that it seems like marrying one's mother-in-law, and likewise a father-in-law should not marry his son-in-law's wife since it seems like marrying his own daughter. And although there is one who wrote that if his wife dies he is permitted to marry the wife of his father-in-law who is not his wife's mother, there are halachic authorities who cast doubt on this. Therefore one must rule that even if his wife has died, it is forbidden for him to marry his father-in-law's wife.
takeaways: By strict law, one is permitted to marry the wife of a father-in-law who is not the mother of one's wife, as in the case of David and Rizpah
There are those who forbid this on account of the appearance that it seems like marrying one's mother-in-law
In practice, the ruling is to forbid it even if one's wife has died

paragraphs: A man is permitted to marry the wife of his brother's son and the wife of his sister's son, and we do not issue a decree on account of his brother's wife, since the generation has been separated.

clarification.explanation: It is permitted for a man to marry the wife of his brother's son and the wife of his sister's son, and no decree is issued regarding them on account of the prohibition of a brother's wife, because the relationship has already become more distant in that generation.
takeaways: It is permitted to marry the wife of one's brother's son or the wife of one's sister's son
No decree is issued regarding them on account of a brother's wife, because of the distance of the generation

paragraphs: The Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote in chapter 2 of the Laws of Forbidden Relations, halachah 14, that a man may marry a woman and her sister's daughter, or her brother's daughter, at the same time. And the Maggid Mishneh wrote that this is simple and clear from the Mishnah in chapter 3 of Keritot — see there. However, from the book HaPardes, attributed to Rashi, of blessed memory, which was brought in the book Hon Yosef Zamaro, siman 9, it appears that a man is forbidden to marry the daughter of his wife's sister during his wife's lifetime. And the author, of blessed memory, was puzzled by this ruling, and the Gaon Maharam Suzin, of blessed memory, answered him that by strict law it is permitted, but a decree was issued regarding this on account of appearances — see there. And although his words are somewhat forced in this, since we have no authority to issue decrees on our own initiative, nevertheless a great man has spoken this matter, and it deserves consideration.

clarification.explanation: The Rambam wrote that a man marries a woman and her sister's daughter or her brother's daughter together, and this ruling is simple and explained in the Mishnah. But the book HaPardes, attributed to Rashi, implies that it is forbidden for a man to marry the daughter of his wife's sister during his wife's lifetime. And Maharam Suzin answered that by strict law it is permitted, but that a decree was issued on this on account of appearances. And although his words are somewhat forced, since we have no authority to issue decrees on our own, nevertheless since a great authority stated this matter, it deserves consideration.
takeaways: According to the Rambam, it is permitted to marry a woman and her sister's daughter or her brother's daughter together
There is a source implying a prohibition on the daughter of a wife's sister during the wife's lifetime
It was suggested that the prohibition is on account of appearances, and it deserves consideration

paragraphs: The Gaon, our teacher Rabbi David Pardo, of blessed memory, in the book Mizmor LeDavid, siman 179, brought in the name of our master the Ari, of blessed memory, that it is not good for a man to marry a woman whose name is the same as his mother's name — see there. And this matter is not found in the writings of our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, that are available to us, but the Rav, of blessed memory, is trustworthy in this testimony that he found it so. And it is known that this matter is also written in Sefer Chasidim among other things, and there it also mentions the case where the groom and his father-in-law share the same name. However, the wording of our master, of blessed memory, who used the phrase "not good," etc., suggests that this caution is a weak one, and one might say that its reason is specifically out of respect. In any case, since this caution was written in the name of our master the Ari, it is proper to be careful about it; but if he changed the name, there is no concern at all. And in the cautions of Sefer Chasidim I have written nothing here, but with God's help I will write, if God wills it.

clarification.explanation: Rabbi David Pardo, in the book Mizmor LeDavid, brought in the name of the Ari that it is not good for a man to marry a woman whose name is the same as his mother's name. This matter is not found in the writings of the Ari available to us, but the Rav is trustworthy in his testimony that he found it so, and it is likewise written in Sefer Chasidim, which also mentions the case where the groom and his father-in-law share the same name. However, the wording "not good" indicates that this caution is a light one, and perhaps its reason is only out of respect for parents. Nevertheless, since it was written in the name of the Ari, it is proper to be careful about it, but if the name was changed, there is no concern at all.
takeaways: There is a caution in the name of the Ari not to marry a woman whose name is the same as one's mother's name
The caution is light, and its reason may be a matter of respect for parents
If the name was changed, there is no concern
